title: Ang 361–365: Guru Amar Das in Asa
tomorrow: what did the fourth Guru write for Sikh weddings?

segments.voice: Yesterday, he named it: Guru Nanak naming the harm out loud, even to God. A page on, the third Guru's voice comes into Asa.

Gardeners say it plainly: a seed kept in the packet stays a seed. It has to go into the dark and come apart before anything green shows up. Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, has his own version of that, and it isn't about seeds. His hymns in Asa begin on ang 361, and a phrase runs through his writing that sounds harsh at first: to die through the Word.
screen: `A SEED IN THE PACKET STAYS A SEED.` → `INTO THE DARK FIRST.` → `TO DIE THROUGH THE WORD?`

segments.voice: The phrase is sabad marai: to die through the Shabad, the Guru's Word. What dies isn't the person. It's haumai, the ego: the voice that says me first, my way, look at me. In Guru Amar Das's hymns, the one who lets that die isn't left empty. That person comes alive to the Name and finds peace. Underneath sits an old human question: how do you get free of yourself? A neighbor tradition asks it too. In the Gospel of John, Jesus says, in the King James words: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.” Both pictures say something has to end so that something truer can live. That's real common ground. And here's an honest difference. Christians read the grain of wheat first as Jesus himself, his own death and rising, which his followers are invited to share. For Guru Amar Das, what dies is the ego, through the Guru's Word, while you're alive: here, now, at the next meal and the next argument. Each says it in its own words, and neither needs the other to be wrong.
screen: `SABAD MARAI: DIE THROUGH THE WORD.` · `WHAT DIES IS HAUMAI, THE EGO.` · `A GRAIN OF WHEAT, IN JOHN.` · `COMMON GROUND, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `THE THIRD GURU.`

segments.voice: Read a hymn on ang 362 if you can. Then sit and let your head bow a little, chin toward your chest, shoulders soft: the posture of someone not trying to be first. Stay there for the sit, and each time a me-first thought comes, let it go back into the ground.
Ang 361. The page where Guru Amar Das's hymns in Raag Asa begin.
Keep this: the third guru, and the ego that goes into the ground so something truer can grow. See you soon.
